description_block:
Gertrude Abercrombie
(American, 1909-1977)
Alderman Merriam's Shells, 1951
oil on masonite in original frame
signed Abercrombie and dated (lower left); titled (on label affixed to reverse)

8 x 11 in.

Property from a Private Collection

This lot is located in New York.
We are grateful for the research conducted by Susan Weininger, Professor Emerita, Roosevelt University.Provenance:Gifted by the Artist to Dr. John T. Reynolds, Kalamazoo, Michigan in exchange for medical services in 1952.Acquired from the estate of the above by the present owner.Exhibited:New York, Edwin Hewitt Gallery, 1952.Chicago, Newman Brown Gallery, 1952.Chicago, Stevens-Gross Gallery, 1952.Milwaukee, Bresler Gallery, 1952.Evanston, Illinois, Contemporary Arts Gallery, 1953.Chicago, Design Center, 1953.Lot Note:This is an exquisite work by Gertrude Abercrombie, depicting a group of shells from the collection of Robert Merriam. Merriam served as the Chicago Alderman of the 5th ward from 1947-55, which included the Hyde Park neighborhood where Abercrombie lived for most of her life. Although Merriam was not in the artist’s inner circle, they certainly knew each other. By the time this painting was made, she was a well-known resident of the neighborhood, and a regular participant in the recently initiated 57th Street Art Fair. Abercrombie’s presence at the fair, with her old Rolls Royce parked nearby, as well as her regular appearances in the community attired in a peaked cap that made her resemble a witch, caught the attention of many in the community. A photograph taken at the 1952 57th St. Fair (fig. 1) of the artist and her husband, Frank Sandiford, with Oliver Merriam, the Alderman’s son, and the old Rolls Royce behind them, indicates that Abercrombie and the Alderman were well acquainted by this time.She also had a long relationship with Merriam’s successor, Leon Despres, who served as her attorney and owned a number of her paintings. Alderman Merriam’s Shells was completed in late 1951, and, according to Abercrombie’s own records, given early in 1952 to Dr. John Reynolds as payment for an operation. The painting retains a sticker from an exhibition originally taped to the frame identifying the artwork’s title and Dr. Reynolds as the lender. It also carries an inscription originally on the paper backing that reads, “From John T. Reynolds.”Alderman Merriam’s Shells has an extensive exhibition history that begins in April 1952, a year in which Abercrombie was the subject of a remarkable five solo shows. That year the painting was exhibited at Edwin Hewitt Gallery in New York; Stevens-Gross Gallery and Newman Brown Gallery in Chicago; and Bresler Gallery in Milwaukee. In 1953, it was exhibited at her solo shows at the Contemporary Arts Gallery in Evanston and the Design Center in Chicago. The Newman Brown exhibit was the subject of “Likes to Paint Simple things which are a Little Strange” (Chicago Sunday Tribune, September 14, 1952), in which Alderman Merriam’s Shells is pictured along with the actual shells that were its subjects, as well as a number of other paintings in the exhibition (fig. 2). The painting was offered for sale in a number of these venues, at prices ranging from $50-$150. One might conclude that Dr. Reynolds would have been willing to sell it if an offer was made; however, the painting was purchased by the current owner this year at a Michigan estate sale. There is no doubt as to the authenticity of this work, and it possesses a very interesting history.Abercrombie’s interest in shells was probably inspired by her good friend John Wilde, a Wisconsin native who, like her, was a figurative artist with a surreal bent. Wilde valued craft and precision, and his work was as finished and refined as the Renaissance artists he admired. It was probably through him that Abercrombie was introduced to Edwin Hewitt, a New York gallerist who showed Magic Realist art. As noted above, Alderman Merriam’s Shells was exhibited in her single exhibition there in 1952, but Hewitt never showed her work again, which suggests she was producing too much too quickly, thus implying a sloppiness. Wilde suggested that she focus on details and precision in her work, something she had trouble doing consistently, particularly when she had to meet deadlines for the many exhibitions to which she was committed in the early 1950s. Abercrombie struggled with these stylistic issues and wrote to Wilde in late 1951 that she was, “giving up trying to be real,” but she “wish[ed] he could see her shells.” A beautiful, highly detailed painting of shells on a beach by Wilde from 1951 (now in the Madison Museum of Contemporary Art), was in her estate, and it must have provided first-hand inspiration.The early 1950s was one of Abercrombie’s most productive periods; she worked assiduously, necessitated at least in part by concerns over money. Her marriage to Bob Livingston, a lawyer and good provider, ended in 1948. She then married Frank Sandiford, a reformed small-time criminal turned record store salesperson, which changed her economic situation. As a result, the artist produced numerous tiny paintings, often of single shells, that were sometimes made into pins or brooches with frames of her design fabricated by a jeweler. These were sold at local art fairs as well as other exhibition venues to make ends meet. Abercrombie almost certainly accumulated a collection of shells of her own after using Alderman Merriam’s as models for the present painting. A number of varieties recur regularly in her work, many of which appear in the borrowed collection. The conch, the snail shell, and the auger (depicted in the painting pinned to an imaginary wall) appear in her work both individually and in more complex compositions, in paintings that range in size from tiny to large (for Abercrombie). Like the many other things she painted consistently—cats, owls, stoneware vessels, Victorian furniture—shells became personal emblems. Throughout the artist’s career, she painted rooms, usually spare and ascetic, closed and impenetrable, which resonated with her own feelings of loneliness and insecurity. Abercrombie also did many paintings in which tents, a more precarious kind of enclosure, feature prominently. The shell is another kind of home, at once protective and confining, a contained space that may have also appealed to Abercrombie thematically. She even played with this idea in her compositions that depict a woman, rather than a snail, emerging from a shell (see In and Out, 1966, Private Collection, and For Once in my Life, 1969, Private Collection) or having an owl or an eye peek out of a small round shell hole. These works, among others, display the artist’s visual wit. While Abercrombie was certainly capable of making a perspectival image in which objects appear to exist in a believable environment, Alderman Merriam’s Shells shows a more abstract, liminal space. The artist depicts the individual shells with careful detail, each of which occupies their own space and displays the view that is most characteristic of the object’s individual personality. They seem to almost float on the surface of the painting until the auger is reached. Hanging above the other shells on their planar surface, it is pinned firmly to a deep black backdrop, an indicator that what appears to be infinite is in fact not. Each impossibly positioned to its best angle on the surface, the shells seem to glimmer in their own aureole light source. And yet, as in all of the best Abercrombie compositions, it feels completely balanced, beautifully composed, and replete with the mystery and simple “strangeness” of her finest work.

description_block:
Roger Brown
(American, 1941-1997)
Michigan Color Watch, 1981
oil on canvas

42 x 65 in.

Property from a Distinguished Private Collection

This lot is located in New York.
Provenance:Phyllis Kind Gallery, New York.Pace Gallery, New York.Acquired from the above by the present owner, 1982.Lot Note: By 1981, Roger Brown had begun dividing his time between Chicago and New Buffalo, Michigan, where he was constructing a lakeside studio on the dunes overlooking Lake Michigan—a vantage point that sharpened his attention to the region's shifting weather and light. Michigan Color Watch distills that close observation into Brown's distinct graphic idiom: a band of dense, scalloped storm clouds, rendered in the interlocking, quilt-like pattern that recurs throughout his skyscapes, presses down over a foreground screen of flattened black silhouettes—sumac fronds, seed heads, and cattails—through which a narrow strip of turquoise water is just visible. A spider and a scattering of insects, picked out in fine detail among the foliage, animate the composition's near-heraldic stillness.As the critic Robert Storr observed of Brown's work, the artist had a gift for making his darker fixations "snappy, mesmerizing, bleakly hilarious and indelible" (R. Storr, "Message and Murmurs from the (Broken) Heartland," in Roger Brown: The American Landscape, exh. cat., DC Moore Gallery, New York, 2008). That tension is indeed fully present here: a sky heavy with implied menace, rendered with the crisp, decorative control of folk art and comic-strip line. The painting's title points to Brown's daily ritual of tracking atmospheric change—translating direct observation of a specific place into an image that is both documentary and highly stylized. Thus, it marks Brown's singular position among the Chicago Imagists, bridging vernacular American subject matter with a disciplined, near-abstract sense of pattern and design.

description_block:
Alex Katz
(American, b. 1927)
Swimmer #2, 1973
oil on linen
signed Alex Katz and dated 8-73 (canvas overhang)

34 x 48 in.

Property from the Collection of Susanne Inez Steinberg

This lot is located in New York.
Provenance:Marlborough Godard, Toronto.Acquired from the above by the present owner, 1976.Lot Note: Painted in 1973, Swimmer #2 belongs to a distinctive moment in Katz’s career, when he was refining the cool, distilled visual language that would come to define his oeuvre. The composition presents a close-cropped profile of his son, Vincent, emerging from rippling water, rendered in luminous planes of color and sweeping, gestural brushwork. The swimmer’s serene expression contrasts with the energetic strokes of water surrounding him, creating a delicate balance between stillness and movement.Throughout the 1970s, Katz returned to the swimmer motif in a small group of related works, including the oils Swimmer and Swimmer #3, both painted in 1973, as well as the prints The Swimmer (1974) and Olympic Swimmer (1976). Across these works, Katz explored repetition and variation, transforming an ordinary moment of leisure into an image of striking graphic clarity and intimacy.Within this small body of work, Swimmer #2 has remained remarkably elusive. While related compositions have entered museums and collections and the imagery has circulated in print, this painting has remained in the same private collection since it was acquired directly from Marlborough Godard, Toronto, in 1976. Its return to public view nearly fifty years later offers a rare opportunity to encounter a work that has - until now - remained largely unseen.

Paul P. 
(Canadian, b. 1977)
Untitled, 2009
oil on canvas
signed Paul P and dated (on the reverse); signed again and dated (on the stretcher)

This lot is located in New York.
Provenance:Daniel Reich Gallery, New York. Acquired from the above by the present owner, 2009.Lot Note:Paul P. has emerged over the past two decades as one of the most distinctive figurative painters of his generation, carving out a body of work that reclaims a nineteenth-century portrait tradition—Whistler, Sargent—for subject matter that tradition would never have countenanced. Since his earliest exhibitions in the early 2000s, drawing on appropriated photographs from the Canadian Lesbian and Gay Archives and pre-AIDS-era gay pornography, he has built a practice around the act of historical recuperation: taking images pushed to the margins and returning them to a lineage of painted portraiture with total sincerity, no irony intended. That project has earned him a place in the permanent collections of The Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, the National Gallery of Canada, LACMA, and the Brooklyn Museum, as well as a spot in the 2014 Whitney Biennial.This work, from 2009, comes from the period in which that reputation was consolidating—the same year P. appeared in a group show at The Museum of Modern Art, shortly before institutional recognition abroad followed at the Institut Valencià d'Art Modern and, later, the Freud Museum in London. What distinguishes P. within contemporary figurative painting is less a signature style than a sustained argument: that desire, memory, and art history are inseparable, and that a painter working today can still make that case through the languid, atmospheric means of an earlier century. As he has put it, his subjects are "anonymous and interchangeable" figures through which he searches for "the touching of hands between the past and the present"—a line that could stand as a statement of purpose for his practice as a whole.

Those familiar with the Post-War New York art scene may recognize the family name: Louis H. Rosenthal, the patriarch of the collection, was the longtime proprietor of Rosenthal's Art & Hobby Supply Company in Greenwich Village, later continuing at New York Central Art Supply Company. For over four decades, Rosenthal was not only a supplier of materials, but a trusted friend and advisor to a generation of artists whose work would come to define the modern and Abstract movements of the 20th century — among them Willem de Kooning, Jackson Pollock, Alice Baber, Esteban Vicente, Mary Abbott, Milton Resnick, Karel Appel, and Paul Jenkins.Before their breakthroughs, many artists of the period were still working with limited means. In such cases, it was not uncommon for these artists to trade their work with Louis in exchange for the very materials that later shaped their successes. The present lot, then, stands as a testament to the Rosenthal family's unique contributions, both material and personal, to the Post-War New York artistic community.

Levy.Gifted by the Trustees of the Corcoran Gallery of Art to the present owner.Exhibited:Philadelphia, Locks Gallery, Thomas Chimes: Faustroll: Landscape, February 25 - April 5, 2003.Literature: Thomas Chimes, Faye Hirsch, and Locks Gallery, Thomas Chimes: Faustroll Landscape, 1980-1990, exhibition catalogue, Philadelphia, 2003, p. 8, no. 9, illustrated.Lot Note:Thomas Chimes’s career was marked by distinct periods of artistic exploration: the Crucifixion Paintings, Metal Boxes, Panel Portraits, and White Paintings. In 1979, Chimes stood at a pivotal moment between two of these periods, having completed his series of Panel Portraits and facing an artistic crisis over what might follow. This period of uncertainty coincided with a painful personal moment, as Chimes separated from his wife.During this difficult time, Chimes moved his studio to the former studio of fellow Philadelphia artist Tommy Dale Palmore, who had hung a large gessoed canvas over the windows to control the light and view. Chimes was captivated by its buttery, layered surface and purchased the canvas from Palmore when he moved in, finding renewed inspiration in its possibilities.Moving away from the intricate detail of his Panel Portraits, Chimes returned to the painted surface, as he had previously explored in his Crucifixion series, while seeking a more immediate and spontaneous approach to painting.He quickly covered his first large canvas in aquamarine blue, which became the basis for his first Waterfall painting. The subject drew upon memories of a happier period in his marriage, when the couple had visited Niagara Falls, while also engaging with the tradition of landscape painting represented by artists including Albert Bierstadt, Thomas Moran, John Henry Twachtman, and J. M. W. Turner.For Chimes, the waterfall became both a site of ethereal natural beauty and a vehicle for personal reflection, embodying the sense of change that defined this crucial moment in his life and career. The present, particularly expansive canvas captures this decisive shift, marking the emergence of a new direction in Chimes’s practice.

Lot Note:David Reed’s #25 belongs to the artist’s early Brushstroke paintings, a seminal series in which he explored the tension between spontaneous gesture and disciplined process. Working wet-into-wet, Reed applied broad strokes of oil paint across tall, narrow canvases in a single, rapid movement. The dimensions of these early works were determined in part by the limits of Reed’s own body- the canvas height corresponded to the door of his studio, while their width was dictated by the reach of his arm. In this way, #25 becomes a record not only of a painted gesture but of the artist’s physical presence, tracing the distance his body could traverse in a single movement.

tempera on canvas

Provenance:Collection of the Brazilian politician Esmerino Arruda.By descent to his grandson.Private Collection, Brazil, acquired from the above.Lot Note:Francisco Domingos da Silva, known as Chico da Silva, was a self-taught Brazilian artist whose work emerged from the popular culture of Fortaleza, Ceará. Illiterate throughout his life, Silva began drawing around 1937 with charcoal, chalk, and fragments of brick on the whitewashed walls of dwellings at Praia Formosa, a neighborhood along Fortaleza’s waterfront. He subsequently transferred his imagery to paper and board, working primarily in gouache and tempera before turning to acrylic and, later, oil on canvas. His early works were signed “F. D. Silva,” frequently accompanied by a thumbprint.Silva developed a repertoire of fantastical, whimsical creatures and hybrid forms, including dragons, birds, snakes, and flying fish. These motifs recur throughout his oeuvre, rendered in saturated, flat areas of color and organized within densely populated compositions. His working process was direct and intuitive; he typically worked without preliminary studies, building compositions through rapidly applied fields of color and distinctive stippling produced by loading his brush with multiple pigments. As Silva explained in 1966, he imagined “the fish and the birds in motion” before developing their colors. Over the course of his career, he worked on diverse surfaces, from walls, paper, and board to canvas, as well as cloth, plywood, and household objects.The immediacy of Silva’s process and his highly personal imagery distinguish his work within twentieth-century Brazilian art. Drawing upon vernacular traditions and his own fantastical imagination rather than academic conventions, he developed a visual language that occupies a compelling space between popular, folk, and self-taught art. His paintings, with their vibrant colors and teeming cast of imaginary creatures, transform the picture plane into an exuberant world of perpetual movement. Today, his paintings are held in major public collections, including Tate, the Museu de Arte do Rio, and the Museu de Arte da Universidade Federal do Ceará.

description_block:
Chris Ofili
(British, b. 1968)
Untitled (Man and Woman), 2003
gold leaf, gouache, and charcoal on paper
signed Chris Ofili and dated (verso)

12 3/8 x 9 3/8 in.

Property from a Distinguished Private Collection

This lot is located in New York.
Provenance:Victoria Miro Gallery, London.Acquired from the above by the present owner, 2003.Lot Note:Chris Ofili’s works on paper have long run concurrent with his paintings and sculpture—not as preparatory sketches, but as fully realized statements in their own right. The Afromuses, a series of small-format watercolors created between 1995 and 2005, form the core of this practice: daily, meditative studies completed in a single sitting, each confined to the same modest scale and the same basic armature—hair, face, neck, and chest, seen frontally or in profile. Within that self-imposed discipline, Ofili found room for continual invention in color, pattern, and technique, with each figure emerging as a distinct study in adornment, hairstyle, and Black identity, drawn from memory, popular culture, and art history rather than any single sitter.Elsewhere in his works on paper, Ofili pushes past watercolor’s immediacy into richer, more ceremonial registers—charcoal set against gold leaf and gouache, for instance, lends a devotional, almost iconic weight to subjects like the recurring pairing of a man and woman, a study in intimacy and courtship that runs throughout this body of work.What unites these works across medium and mood is Ofili’s consistent instinct toward beauty as strategy: "I try to make [my work] more and more beautiful, to decorate it and dress it up so that it is so irresistible, you just want to be in front of it" (C. Ofili, quoted in L. Macritchie, "Ofili’s Glittering Icons—Work of Chris Ofili at the Brooklyn Museum of Art, New York," Art in America, January 2000). Whether in the bloom of a watercolor wash or the shimmer of burnished gold, that pursuit of surface seduction is what gives even his smallest, most intimate works their compelling nature. Ofili’s work holds a firm place in major institutional collections, including the Museum of Modern Art, New York; Tate, London; the British Museum, London; the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles; and the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, among others—a testament to the critical and curatorial consensus behind an artist whose market remains comparatively concentrated in a small number of headline works.

painted nickel silver on a leather covered wooden plinth

This lot is located in New York.
Provenance: Contemporary Fine Arts, Berlin.Acquired from the above by the present owner, 2005.Literature: Berlin, Contemporary Fine Arts, The Blue Rider: Chris Ofili, exhibition catalogue, 2005, p. 27, illustrated (edition number unknown). Lot Note: Half Moon (Blue) dates to 2005, the year Ofili made his debut as a sculptor with The Blue Rider, an exhibition at Contemporary Fine Arts, Berlin, staged in the wake of his acclaimed presentation in the British Pavilion at the Venice Biennale and the unveiling of The Upper Room at Tate. For that body of work, Ofili restricted himself to a tightly controlled palette of blue and silver, deploying patinated surfaces in place of the layered color and glitter of his paintings—a chromatic discipline that gave the exhibition its name and unified painting and sculpture alike. The sculptures took as their starting point the Catalan tradition of the caganer—a squatting, defecating figure tucked into nativity scenes as an irreverent note of earthy humanity amid the sacred—a reference that extends Ofili's long-standing, deliberately provocative use of scatological imagery, most notoriously in his elephant-dung-inflected paintings of the 1990s.As Ofili has explained of these figures: "It's what they symbolize that interests me. The sculptures are a dialogue — about relationships, about how people can be both intensely connected and entirely at ease with one another" (C. Ofili, quoted in Chris Ofili: Silver Moon, Tatintsian Gallery, Moscow). Cast in blue, Half Moon (Blue) stands as the cooler-toned counterpart within this small body of sculpture—its deep, night-inflected surface anticipating the blue palette that would come to define Ofili's paintings following his move to Trinidad that same year—while carrying forward the same interest in the body, relationship, and ritual as sites where the sacred and the profane meet.

ink and gouache on paper

(However the subject couldn’t be more different: an impoverished young woman taunted by village locals.) Bonosky was a lifelong, dedicated Communist who would later, at Neel’s behest, help organize a show of her work in the Soviet Union in 1981, just three years before her death. This lot is located in New York.
Provenance: Gaga, Mexico City.Private Collection.Lot Note:Since the early 2000s, Cosima von Bonin has developed a body of textile wall works—sewn rather than painted, and typically fabricated by master seamstresses to her design—that recast the language of geometric abstraction in soft, pieced fabric. Von Bonin refers to these works as "Lappen" (rags, or cloths), a term whose modesty is itself part of the gesture, deflating painting's traditional claims to authorship and craft even as the works occupy its wall-based, framed format. The recurring "Bubbles" motif, seen across related Lappen, such as 36 Bubbles Loop (2010), reduces the field to a pattern of stitched, circular forms: a deadpan nod to hard-edge abstraction and Pop repetition, rendered through sewing and patchwork rather than paint. Halfway Bubbles 1, 2, and 3 extends this inquiry across three panels, its title's "halfway" suggesting an interrupted or partial version of the pattern, in keeping with von Bonin's ongoing interest in exhaustion, incompletion, and irony as both formal and conceptual strategies. Exhibited within the same year as major surveys of her work at the Arnolfini, MAMCO Geneva, and Museum Ludwig, Cologne, the triptych reflects a period in which von Bonin's Lappen stood alongside her sculptural practice as a central, and increasingly recognized, strand of her work. Von Bonin's work holds a place in major international collections, including Tate, London; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles; the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam; and the Museum für Neue Kunst im ZKM, Karlsruhe.
